title: Should Christians Keep the Sabbath?
excerpt: The fourth commandment is the longest of the ten and the one Christians agree on least. Some hold that the Sabbath continues on Sunday, some that Christ fulfilled it and the day is free, and some that the seventh day still binds. Each view is given in its own confession's words, with a word for the tired.
body:
A nurse works every other Sunday, and an aunt has told her more than once that she is breaking the fourth commandment. A man grew up in a house where Sunday meant stiff clothes, no ball games and a long silent afternoon, and he now spends the day like any other and can't tell whether what he feels about it is freedom or guilt. A woman has started attending a church that meets on Saturday, and her family thinks she has joined something strange. A father of three has not had a full day off in seven weeks, and he would settle for any day at all.

The skeptic has noticed something about the Ten Commandments. Christians hang them on walls and defend nine of them. The one they have quietly let go is the only one that orders a day of rest, and those who do keep it can't agree on which day it is.

He has a point. Faithful Christians have held three different positions on it for centuries, and each of them is written into confessions that whole churches still teach.

## The Longest Commandment

The fourth commandment is the longest of the ten. "Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days you shall labor, and do all your work, but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the Lord your God" (Exodus 20:8-10). Exodus gives creation as the reason: "in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them, and rested on the seventh day" (Exodus 20:11). When Moses repeats the commandment forty years later he gives a second reason. The day is for the whole household, down to the animals and the foreigner, "that your male servant and your female servant may rest as well as you. You shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt" (Deuteronomy 5:14-15).

That second reason explains a good deal. The people who first received this law had been brickmakers for a king who gave no days off. A weekly stop, guaranteed to the lowest worker in the house, told them they were no longer owned. Israel had been given the day before it was given the law, in the wilderness, when the manna fell double on the sixth morning and not at all on the seventh. Later it is called a sign of the covenant: "the people of Israel shall keep the Sabbath, observing the Sabbath throughout their generations, as a covenant forever" (Exodus 31:16).

The prophets treated the day as a test of the heart. Amos heard merchants asking when it would be over, "that we may offer wheat for sale," with rigged scales ready (Amos 8:5). Isaiah promised joy to those who "call the Sabbath a delight" (Isaiah 58:13).

## A Living Practice

Before Christians argue about the Sabbath they should remember that it belongs to someone. From Friday evening until Saturday evening the Jewish people keep it, and have kept it through every century of the church's existence. It is a living practice, and it didn't end where the Old Testament ends.

Christian preaching has often described that practice as a mass of petty rules that Jesus came to sweep away. The Study Bible's study of the Sabbath on this site warns against exactly this. "Christians should not caricature Judaism here," it says, and it points out that Jewish teachers also held that saving a life overrides the Sabbath, and that a saying close to one of Jesus's own is preserved in rabbinic writings. The same study mentions a book by a Jewish philosopher of the last century that "described the day as a sanctuary built in time rather than space," and that many Christians have read. Whatever Christians conclude about their own duty, they have no business sneering at a day their neighbors have kept at great cost.

## Jesus and the Sabbath

Jesus kept the Sabbath. Luke says that at Nazareth, "as was his custom, he went to the synagogue on the Sabbath day" (Luke 4:16). The Gospels also record more arguments about this commandment than about any other, and all sides in the Christian debate appeal to them.

When his disciples plucked heads of grain on their way through the grainfields and were accused of breaking the Sabbath, he answered, "The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath. So the Son of Man is lord even of the Sabbath" (Mark 2:27-28). In a synagogue, with a man's withered hand in front of him, he asked, "Is it lawful on the Sabbath to do good or to do harm, to save life or to kill?" (Mark 3:4). When he straightened a woman who had been bent double for eighteen years, and the ruler of the synagogue objected, he asked whether she ought not "be loosed from this bond on the Sabbath day" (Luke 13:16). For him the day of rest was the right day to set someone free.

What do these stories show? Those who believe the commandment still binds point out that Jesus never broke it and never said it was ending. He stripped away its abuse and gave it back as a gift, "made for man." Those who believe it has been fulfilled point to the other half of the sentence. He calls himself its lord, and in Matthew the argument in the grainfield follows directly on his invitation, "Come to me, all who labor and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Matthew 11:28). On this reading he was claiming to be what the day had pointed to all along.

One more detail belongs to every reading. After he was buried, the women who had followed him went home, and "on the Sabbath they rested according to the commandment" (Luke 23:56). He rose the next morning, on the first day of the week.

## Three Sentences of Paul

Paul speaks to the matter three times. To the Romans, in a chapter about disputes between believers, he writes, "One person esteems one day as better than another, while another esteems all days alike. Each one should be fully convinced in his own mind" (Romans 14:5). To the Colossians: "let no one pass judgment on you in questions of food and drink, or with regard to a festival or a new moon or a Sabbath. These are a shadow of the things to come, but the substance belongs to Christ" (Colossians 2:16-17). And he worries over the Galatians because they "observe days and months and seasons and years" (Galatians 4:10) as part of going back to the law as their standing with God.

It is also worth noticing a silence. When the apostles met in Jerusalem to decide what to require of Gentile converts, they sent a short list (Acts 15:28-29), and the Sabbath is not on it.

Those who hold that the day is now free take these sentences as they stand. Those who hold that the Sabbath continues on Sunday reply that Paul is speaking of the Jewish calendar, the seventh day with its festivals and new moons, and that the Lord's Day is not in view. Those who keep the seventh day reply that the Sabbaths Paul calls a shadow are the ceremonial feast days of Israel's year, and that the weekly Sabbath of the Ten Commandments is a different thing. Each reading is possible, and each has to work harder at one of the three sentences than at the others.

The letter to the Hebrews adds a line that all of them claim: "there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God" (Hebrews 4:9).

## The First Day

The New Testament shows Christians gathering on the first day of the week. At Troas, "on the first day of the week, when we were gathered together to break bread," Paul preached until midnight (Acts 20:7). He told the Corinthians to set money aside "on the first day of every week" (1 Corinthians 16:2). John had his vision "on the Lord's day" (Revelation 1:10).

The earliest writings after the New Testament say the same. The Didache, a manual of church practice written late in the first century or in the early second, tells believers that on every Lord's day they are to "gather yourselves together, and break bread." Ignatius of Antioch, writing around 110, describes believers brought up in the old order as "no longer observing the Sabbath," and living by the Lord's Day. Justin, explaining Christian worship to the emperor about the year 155, wrote, "Sunday is the day on which we all hold our common assembly," and gave two reasons, that it was the first day of creation and the day Jesus rose. An early writing called the Epistle of Barnabas says, "we keep the eighth day with joyfulness, the day also on which Jesus rose again from the dead."

Two cautions go with this evidence. The first is about what it shows. These writers describe a day of gathering. None of them calls Sunday the Sabbath, and none describes it as a day off work. The site's study of the Sabbath records that a law of the emperor Constantine in 321 ordered townspeople to rest on Sunday, and that "for centuries some Christians, especially in the East, continued to honor Saturday alongside Sunday."

The second caution is about us. The church's move away from the seventh day was mixed with contempt for the people who kept it. A council at Laodicea in the fourth century ruled that "Christians must not judaize by resting on the Sabbath, but must work on that day," honoring the Lord's Day instead, "and, if they can, resting then as Christians." It attached a curse for those who disobeyed. Historians argue about how much that contempt had to do with the change of day. The canon's own wording shows that it was involved.

## Three Answers

The first answer is that the Sabbath continues, on the first day. This is the teaching of the Westminster Confession of 1646 and of the Presbyterian and Baptist churches that follow it. God, it says, "by a positive, moral, and perpetual commandment, binding all men in all ages," has "appointed one day in seven for a Sabbath." From creation to the resurrection that day was the last of the week, and "from the resurrection of Christ, was changed into the first day of the week," which it calls "the Christian Sabbath." The day is to be spent in worship and in "the duties of necessity and mercy." The conviction underneath is that the Ten Commandments are God's permanent moral law and that the fourth is not the odd one out. It rests on creation, before there was an Israel. What this view fears is a church that has declared one of the ten optional, and a world in which nobody's rest is protected. Its hard question is where the New Testament says the day was changed.

The second answer is that the Sabbath is fulfilled and the day is free. This is the teaching of the Lutheran confessions and of many other Protestants. Luther's Large Catechism of 1529 says the commandment in its outward sense "does not concern us Christians; for it is altogether an external matter, like other ordinances of the Old Testament." The Augsburg Confession of the next year says flatly, "Scripture has abrogated the Sabbath-day," and explains that the church chose Sunday so that people would know when to come together. A Swiss Reformed confession of the 1560s agrees: "we celebrate the Lord's Day and not the Sabbath as a free observance." The view is older than the Reformation. Thomas Aquinas had taught that Sunday replaced the Sabbath "not by virtue of the precept but by the institution of the Church and the custom of Christian people." None of these writers thought rest unimportant. Luther wanted a day kept so that working people "may retire in order to rest and be refreshed." The conviction underneath is that Christ is the rest the day promised. What this view fears is a new law laid on consciences that Christ set free. Its hard question is why only this one of the Ten Commandments should have expired, when Genesis has God resting on the seventh day long before Sinai.

The third answer is that the seventh day still binds. Seventh Day Baptists have held this since the seventeenth century, and Seventh-day Adventists since the nineteenth. The Adventist statement of belief says that God "instituted the Sabbath for all people as a memorial of Creation," and that "the fourth commandment of God's unchangeable law requires the observance of this seventh-day Sabbath," kept "from evening to evening, sunset to sunset." Those who hold this view don't claim to earn salvation by a day. Their conviction is that God named the day himself, and that no verse of the New Testament moves it. They fear a church that changed a commandment of God on its own authority, and the Augsburg Confession itself reports that defenders of the bishops' power made the change of day their chief example of it. Their hard question is the one Paul's three sentences put to them, together with the evidence that Christians were gathering on the first day well within a century of the resurrection.

The Catholic Church gives an account of its own. As this site's study describes it, Sunday fulfills the Sabbath, and the church, "by the authority Christ gave it," requires worship and rest on that day.

## What Is Settled

Some things are held by all of them. No day earns anyone standing with God. Christians are to gather for worship. Rest is a gift of God and not a weakness. And the day was given for the sake of the worker as much as the owner.

How the fourth commandment binds a Christian now is not settled, and no creed rules on it. It belongs with the matters on which believers may differ and remain in one church, and this essay takes no side among the three. Paul's instruction for such questions was addressed to both parties at once: "Who are you to pass judgment on the servant of another?" (Romans 14:4).

## What We Did with the Day

We have failed in two directions. Where the stricter view ruled, we often turned the gift into a burden. We made lists of what could and could not be done, taught children to dread the day, and judged the neighbor who hung out washing. That is the very thing Jesus was arguing against in the grainfield, done by people who had read the story many times.

Where the freer view ruled, we often kept the freedom and dropped the rest. Sunday became a morning service followed by shopping, and then the service became optional too. People pay for that arrangement, and they are mostly the ones the commandment was written to protect. Someone serves the lunch after church and someone stocks the shelves. Deuteronomy's reason for the day was that the servant "may rest as well as you." The study on this site says that whatever view a Christian holds, the commandment's pattern "asks how their week treats those who work for them, sell to them, and serve them." Amos's merchants only resented the day. We arranged matters so that the poor work straight through it.

## For the Tired

The nurse first. Every one of the three views excuses her. The strictest of the confessions quoted above makes room in its own words for "the duties of necessity and mercy," and the Lord of the Sabbath spent the day healing. No reading of the commandment makes a sin of caring for the sick on a Sunday.

Then the father who has worked seven weeks without a break. Nothing in this essay is a rule for him, and he doesn't need another one. He may need to hear what the commandment was when it was first given. It was spoken to freed slaves, and it told them that the God who had brought them out did not want from them what Pharaoh had wanted. "It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep" (Psalm 127:2). The site's page for the person who is [burned out at work](/help/work-burnout) says of that kind of tiredness that it "isn't laziness, and it isn't a failure of faith; it's what happens to a person who has carried too much for too long with nowhere to set it down." It has small steps for this week, and they are worth more than an argument about days.

Some people can't stop. A mother with two jobs doesn't control her schedule, and telling her to keep a Sabbath only adds to what she carries. Deuteronomy does not speak to her first. Its command goes to the householder, the person with power over other people's time, and it requires him to give his workers their rest. Anyone who employs, manages or is served by other people is the one that commandment is talking to.

On the day after the crucifixion the body of Jesus lay in a tomb, and the women who loved him "rested according to the commandment." He rose at dawn on the first day. Those who keep the seventh day, those who keep the first and those who hold every day alike all find their case somewhere in that one weekend, and they haven't yet agreed about it. The father of three is still tired. He isn't waiting for the argument to be settled, and the invitation Matthew placed just before the story in the grainfield is addressed to people like him, with no day named in it.

*"The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath."* (Mark 2:27)

*"So then, there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God."* (Hebrews 4:9)
